In his opinion for the Court, Chief Justice Roberts addressed three 
significant, issues of relevance to administrative law. (The majority opinion also 
rejected an equal protection challenge to the DACA rescission, which we do not 
discuss further. Justice Sotomayor dissented from that holding.)
First, the majority held that, under the APA’s presumption of 
reviewability, the rescission of DACA was not “committed to agency discretion 
by law.” We will address this topic in more detail in Chapter 8, infra. For 
present purposes, it suffices to note that the Court held that ‘TDACA is not 
simply a non-enforcement policy” that would be committed to “agency 
discretion by law.” The Court gave two reasons. One, the initial DACA 
memorandum directs immigration authorities to “establish a clear and 
efficient process” for identifying eligible individuals and notifying those who 
receive grants. Two, the DACA memorandum had the effect of providing 
recipients benefits, the access of which “courts often are called upon to protect.”
Second, the majority held that the Nielson memorandum was not part of 
the record, but rather a “post hoc rationalization” of the Duke memorandum. 
The Court observed that “[i]t is a ‘foundational principle of administrative law’ 
that judicial review of agency action is limited to ‘the grounds that the agency 
invoked when it took the action.’ ” That means that “[w]hen an agency’s initial 
explanation ‘indicate [s] the determinative reason for the final action taken,’ 
the agency may elaborate later on that reason (or reasons) but may not provide 
new ones.” The Court held that, although Secretary Nielson could have taken 
new agency action upon the D.C. district court’s ruling, she did not do so but 
rather “declin[ed] to disturb the Duke memorandum’s rescission.” According to 
the Court, “the Nielsen Memorandum was by its own terms not a new rule 
implementing a new policy.” Thus, Secretary Nielson was “limited” to the 
“original reasons” given by the Duke memorandum and could not provide an 
“impermissible 'post hoc justification.’ ” That was relevant because the Duke 
memorandum rested on the theory that DACA is unlawful, whereas the 
Nielsen memorandum offered “three ‘separate and independently sufficient 
reasons’ ” for the rescission, including that DACA was legally questionable and 
should be terminated for poHcy reasons and to avoid burdensome litigation. In 
this respect, the Court reasoned that, although “[legal uncertainty” is “related 
to illegality,” the “two justifications are meaningfully distinct,” such that “an 
agency might, for one reason or another, choose to do nothing in the fact of 
uncertainty.” Citing Chenery, the Court reasoned that “[pjermitting agencies 
to invoke belated justifications * * * can upset ‘the orderly functioning of the 
process of review.’ ” The Court acknowledged that it had often invoked this 
principle to limit “what lawyers may argue,” but held that the “functional 
reasons for requiring contemporaneous explanations apply with equal force 
regardless whether post hoc justifications are raised in court by those 
appearing on behalf of the agency or by agency officials themselves.”
